newsitem.title: UK: UK GILTS THIS WEEK - Struggle with strong data ahead.
newsitem.headline: UK GILTS THIS WEEK - Struggle with strong data ahead.

text.p: UK gilts may struggle to make much headway this week with economic data likely to confirm the consumer-led recovery is gathering pace and that interest rates will soon have to rise.
"I can't see the data being anything other than bad news for bonds this week," said Joanne Collins, senior economist at Nomura International.
She said housing starts data on Thursday will confirm the strong recovery in the property market and industrial production figures will show output still on an improving trend.
"Gilts are not going to outperform in a climate like this."
The week got off to a poor start when M0 figures showed a faster-than-expected monthly acceleration in narrow money supply in December.
The 10-year yield spread between gilts and Bunds widened to 193 basis points from 189 on Friday.

The Bund market will have to absorb up to 15 billion marks of new bonds scheduled for auction in the first 10 days of January. But Brian Hilliard, senior international economist at Societe Generale, said there is still not much scope for the yield spread to narrow.
"There isn't much chance the spread will break out of its recent 180 to 200 basis points range," he said. "And stories of renewed political uncertainty are definitely not going to help."

The early days of the new year saw the government rift over Europe widen when Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell adopted a more anti-European Union line, further isolating the few remaining pro-Europeans in the cabinet.
"The key thing for markets is whether or not (Prime Minister John) Major is going to be allowed to hold on until his preferred (election) date of May 1," said one salesman.
Most analysts said the yield curve would remain steady this week with the short end, a recent underperformer, unlikely to fall further.
The short sterling strip is factoring in a series of sharp interest rate rises, starting with a 50 basis points increase by the end of the first quarter.
"The short end has absorbed so much bad news recently it's hard to see it selling off much further," said Hilliard.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George meet on January 15 to discuss monetary policy.
A growing number of analysts expects to see a rate rise following that meeting.
Housing starts figures on Thursday are expected to show another hefty rise in the three months to November, in line with October's 18 percent rise.

The Confederation of British Industry's distributive trades survey early on Friday will provide early evidence of retail sales over the crucial pre- and post-Christmas period. Analysts expect retailers to report healthy, but not booming, sales.
On Friday, offical data for industrial production are due. The Reuter poll forecasts industrial production rose 0.3 percent in November for year-on-year growth of 1.0 percent.
Manufacturing output is forecast to rise 0.2 percent for 1.3 percent year on year.

But domestic data may be quickly overshadowed by events in the U.S. "Gilts are going to be under the cosh of the U.S. as Friday approaches," said the salesman. The key December U.S. non-farm payroll is due on Friday at 1330 GMT and forecast to rise 192,000 compared with 118,000 in November.
